To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the brain involvement is more severe in patients with MS than in patients with systemic immune mediated disease; (b) patients with NSLE show brain damage, which is similar in severity to that observed in patients with MS; (c) in patients with SLE without CNS involvement, brain damage is absent or mild.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MRI and MTI are complementary in detecting brain abnormalities in MS.
brain involvement in systemic immune-mediated diseases is not a common finding, even in the absence of clinical evidence of CNS disease.
MRI lesions in SIDs are macroscopic and MTR changes are microscopic, whereas in MS both are microscopic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brain MRI and MTI are useful tools in the assessment of brain damage in patients with MS and SIDs.
the MTR technique is a useful tool for detecting and quantifying brain damage in patients with MS but not in systemic immune mediated CNS diseases.
brain MRI and MT imaging can provide a useful tool to understand the nature of brain lesions and to monitor the disease progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is involved in systemic immune mediated disease, and the involvement is different from MS.
MTI may be used as a tool for the differential diagnosis of MS and SIDs, as the MTR histogram parameters are different among these groups of patients.
the brain is involved in patients with systemic lupus erythematosis (SLE), and the involvement is not limited to patients with clinical CNS manifestations (NSLE).
